scenario: AITA for telling my mother she is the reason I won't wear white to my wedding? | I'm engaged. Planning on a small semi-formal beach wedding. Mum tells me that she can't wait to go wedding dress shopping with me and she wants to book an appointment at this fancy bridal shop in town. I told mum that I didn't want a white dress and that shop did just white bridal dresses and nothing else (I'd already looked it up). I think the whole concept of white wedding dresses is stupid. It only started with Queen Vic so it's not some ancient tradition and the ship has sailed on the whole white = pure/innocent/virginal thing. However, the main and the defining reason I am anti white wedding dress, is that my mother wore a white dress when she got married, and she and dad are divorced now. Every other woman in my family has worn a coloured dress to get married in (usually either blue or red and either really pale or really dark, with not much in between) and they have all had long (mostly) happy marriages that were either til death did them part or are still going strong today. When mum asked why I didn't want a white dress I first gave the the Queen Vic line which mum said wasn't enough justification, and then the bit about how I'm not exactly "innocent", which was an awful conversation to have with my mother. When she said that wasn't good enough I said "because I just don't want a white dress and I think coloured dresses look nicer and it's my wedding so I get to pick my clothes". Mum asked a few more times what the real reason was and I eventually admitted that her being the only woman to break the tradition and also the only woman to get divorced didn't exactly instill me with confidence in white dresses. Mum got really quiet, then I saw she was crying. She said she tried her best and that I spoke to her like that when I know how the divorce upset her was really cruel. I haven't apologised yet but I feel like she backed me into a corner and wouldn't accept any of the 3 perfectly fine answers I'd given before that, and I shouldn't have had to justify myself to begin with as it is my wedding so the only people whose opinions matter are me and my fiance. I also feel like if she had just accepted my choice or any of the first 3 answers I gave then I would not be in this situation. AITA?

Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether the action in this scenario is morally acceptable or not. Let me read through the scenario again to make sure I understand it properly.

The person is a woman who is engaged and planning a small, semi-formal beach wedding. Her mother wants to go wedding dress shopping together at a specific bridal shop that only does white dresses. The woman doesn't want a white dress and has already looked up the shop, knowing they only do white. She thinks the whole white wedding dress thing is stupid, starting with Queen Victoria, so it's not an ancient tradition. She also mentions that the symbolism of white as pure, innocent, or virginal is outdated.

The main reason she's against a white dress is that her mother wore one and then got divorced. Every other woman in her family wore colored dresses, and their marriages were long and happy. When her mother asked why she didn't want a white dress, she first gave the Queen Victoria line, which her mother dismissed. Then she mentioned not being innocent, which was a tough conversation. Her mother pressed further, and eventually, the woman admitted that her mother being the only one to break the tradition and get divorced made her not confident in white dresses. Her mother got upset, cried, and said that the woman spoke to her cruelly, knowing how the divorce had affected her. The woman hasn't apologized yet and feels like her mother backed her into a corner, making her justify her choice when it's her wedding.

Now, the question is whether the woman's action is morally acceptable. She told her mother that her divorce was the reason she doesn't want a white dress. I need to evaluate if this action is morally acceptable (answer 1) or not (answer 0).

First, I should consider the context. The woman is planning her own wedding and wants to choose her dress. It's her right to make that choice. However, she had to explain her reasons to her mother, who was insistent on knowing why. The woman's reasons were personal and tied to her mother's past, which is sensitive.

On one hand, the woman is asserting her independence and making a choice about her own wedding. She's also honest about her reasons, even though it's difficult. On the other hand, she's bringing up her mother's divorce, which is a painful topic, and doing so in a way that her mother felt was cruel.

I think the key points are:
1. The woman's right to choose her wedding dress.
2. The sensitivity of bringing up her mother's divorce as the reason.
3. The mother's reaction and feelings being hurt.

It's understandable that the woman feels her choice should be respected without having to justify it, especially to her mother. However, when she did justify it, she chose to link it to her mother's past, which was hurtful. While she had the right to make her choice, the way she communicated her reasons was harsh and could be seen as disrespectful or unkind.

Therefore, while her decision to choose a colored dress is her right, the manner in which she explained her reasons, especially tying it to her mother's divorce, might be considered morally unacceptable because it caused emotional harm to her mother.
